metadata.title: Baseline programming diagnostic
metadata.summary: A low-stakes check of starting knowledge before Week 1 teaching. Not a formal OCR assessment and not a grade.

content.text: Before we start
This diagnostic helps you and your teacher see what you already know about software, data and input/output. It does not count toward Assignment 1 or P1.

content.prompt: Which of these is the best description of software used in a workplace?

options.label: A set of programs that store, process or present business information
Only the physical keyboard and screen

feedback.correct: Software is the programs a business uses to handle information.
feedback.incorrect: Think about programs that store or process information, not the hardware or paper records.

content.prompt: Which value is a Boolean?

feedback.correct: Boolean values are True or False.
feedback.incorrect: Boolean means True or False, not text or a number.

content.prompt: In Python, what does input() do?

options.label: Reads text typed by the user

feedback.correct: input() reads text from the user.
feedback.incorrect: print() displays output. input() reads what the user types.

content.prompt: Have you written a program before? If yes, which language? If no, write 'No previous programming'.
content.guidance: Thank you. This is a starting-point note for you and your teacher, not a mark.

content.title: Formative only
content.text: Correct options for these checks are stored in the hub as low-stakes formative material. They are not secure assignment evidence.

metadata.title: Business data explorer
metadata.summary: Connect software in a workplace to the data it stores, then classify business values using integer, floating point, string and Boolean.

content.text: Businesses use software to take orders, store customer details, calculate prices and record whether a delivery is required. Those programs only work if each piece of data has an appropriate type.
A local supplier takes telephone orders. Classify each piece of order data.

content.prompt: Choose the most appropriate fundamental data type for each item.

feedback.correct: Name is text, quantity is a whole number, price may include pence, and delivery is yes/no.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: is it text, a whole number, a number that may include a fraction, or true/false?

content.prompt: Why is a floating point type more appropriate than an integer for a product price?
content.guidance: A price can include a fractional amount, such as 12.50. An integer can only store whole numbers.

content.prompt: Name one workplace system you have seen (till, booking, stock). What data does it store?

content.title: Formative classification
content.text: Expected types are included in this activity JSON for instant feedback. This is not Assignment 1 marking.

metadata.title: Variables and fundamental data types
metadata.summary: Learn what a variable is and when to use integer, floating point, string and Boolean in a business program.

content.text: Unit 14 is internally assessed. Week 1 starts Assignment 1 (P1): explain universal programming constructs with worked examples. Completing this activity is practice, not P1 achieved.
A variable is a named store for a value. The type describes what kind of value it holds.

content.label: Read these Python examples, then add one more variable of your own.

content.prompt: Which fundamental type should store whether an invoice has been paid?

feedback.correct: Paid or not paid is a Boolean.
feedback.incorrect: A yes/no business fact is stored as Boolean.

content.prompt: In your own words, what is the difference between a variable and a value?
content.guidance: A value is the data itself (for example 3). A variable is the named store that holds that value.

metadata.title: Print and input
metadata.summary: Use print to display information and input to capture business data into variables.

content.text: print() shows information to the user. input() reads text the user types and you store it in a variable. Use the agreed Python environment for this unit.

content.label: Python editor
content.instructions: Complete the program so it asks for a product name and prints a confirmation. Do not run untrusted code in the browser; the check looks for input() and print() only.
content.starter:
product_name = input("Product name: ")
# Print a confirmation that includes the product name.
hints: Call input() to capture the name.
Use print() to show the confirmation.

checks.passFeedback: The program uses input, a variable and print. This is formative structure checking, not code execution.
checks.failFeedback: Include input(), store the result in a variable, and use print().

content.prompt: What does input() return in Python?

feedback.correct: input() returns text. Week 2 looks at converting types in more depth.
feedback.incorrect: input() returns text. Whole numbers need a later conversion step.

metadata.title: Guided business-data practice
metadata.summary: Select an appropriate type for several items in a small business scenario and explain at least one choice.

content.text: A cafe records takeaway orders. For each data item, choose a fundamental type.

content.prompt: Classify the cafe order data.

items.label: Customer is on the loyalty scheme

feedback.correct: Names and notes are strings, cup count is an integer, price is floating point, loyalty is Boolean.
feedback.incorrect: Match each value to text, whole number, fractional number, or true/false.

content.prompt: Explain why number of cups is an integer rather than a floating point value.
content.guidance: You cannot sell 2.7 cups in this scenario. A count of cups is a whole number, so integer is appropriate.

metadata.title: First Python business-order program
metadata.summary: Create a simple program that asks for business-order information, stores it in variables and prints a formatted summary.

content.text: Ask for business-order information, store each piece in a variable with an appropriate type, and print a summary. Do not add Week 2 conversion work beyond the int() scaffold for quantity.

content.label: Python editor
content.instructions: Keep the four fundamental types in mind: name as string, quantity as integer, price as a number that may include pence, delivery as a yes/no fact. The browser does not execute this program.
content.starter:
# Business order — Week 1
# input() returns text. int() is used only so quantity is a whole number.

customer_name = input("Customer name: ")
quantity = int(input("Number of items: "))
unit_price = input("Unit price: ")
delivery_required = input("Delivery required (True/False): ")

print("Order summary")
print("Customer:", customer_name)
print("Quantity:", quantity)
print("Unit price:", unit_price)
print("Delivery required:", delivery_required)
hints: Print a labelled summary of all four values.
Commit this file in your GitHub repository, not only in the hub.

checks.passFeedback: The structure uses input, variables and print. Run the file in your Python environment and commit it on GitHub.
checks.failFeedback: Include input(), print(), and variables for the order data.

content.prompt: Which variable was hardest to type, and why?

metadata.title: Homework: extend the business-order program
metadata.summary: Extend the order program with at least six pieces of business data covering all four fundamental types, then commit, push and add to the Assignment 1 guide.

content.text: Independent study: extend the program, use at least six pieces of business data, cover integer, floating point, string and Boolean, commit and push, then extend your Assignment 1 notes.

content.label: Python editor
content.instructions: Work in your cloned repository. The check only looks for input, print and several assignments. It does not execute code or award P1.
content.starter:
# Homework extension — at least six pieces of business data
# Cover string, integer, floating point and Boolean.

customer_name = input("Customer name: ")
product_name = input("Product name: ")
quantity = int(input("Quantity: "))
unit_price = input("Unit price: ")
delivery_required = input("Delivery required (True/False): ")
loyalty_member = input("Loyalty member (True/False): ")

print("Extended order summary")
print(customer_name, product_name, quantity, unit_price, delivery_required, loyalty_member)
hints: Keep all four fundamental types in the data you collect.

checks.passFeedback: The extension still uses input, variables and print. Commit and push on GitHub, then add the example to your technical guide.
checks.failFeedback: Keep input(), print() and several variable assignments.
